title: Ben-Ammi – ancestor of the Ammonites
summary: Lot's youngest daughter bore a son she named Ben-Ammi – a name meaning 'son of my kinsman' in Hebrew, pointing back to the dramatic circumstances surrounding his conception in a cave after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:36–38). This son became the ancestor of the Ammonites, a people who settled east of the Jordan with Rabbah (modern-day Amman) as their center. The narrative has a clear etiological function: it anchors the origin of the Ammonites in kinship with Israel through Lot, Abraham's nephew, while also explaining the ambivalent relationship between the two peoples. That God explicitly forbade the Israelites from attacking the Ammonite territory during the wilderness wanderings (Deut 2:19) testifies to a theological recognition of their right to their own land – a right grounded in Lot's familial bond with Abraham. Nevertheless, subsequent biblical history is marked by repeated conflicts: Ammonite oppression during the period of the judges, warfare under Saul and David, and sharp prophetic judgments from Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Amos. Ben-Ammi thus stands as a link between the patriarchal era and the long, tension-filled history of Israel and its neighboring peoples in Transjordan.
roles: eponym (namesake of the people, the Ammonites)

keyEvents.title: The birth of Ben-Ammi
keyEvents.description: After the destruction of Sodom, Lot fled with his two daughters to a cave in the mountains. The older daughter gave birth to Moab, and the younger gave birth to a son whom she named Ben-Ammi, which means 'son of my kinsman'. He became the ancestor of the Ammonites.

keyEvents.title: God's protection over the land of the Ammonites
keyEvents.description: When the Israelites were traveling toward the Promised Land, God commanded them not to attack or provoke the Ammonites, because he had given this area as an inheritance to Lot's descendants.

keyEvents.title: The oppression of Israel by the Ammonites
keyEvents.description: During the time of the judges, the Ammonites oppressed Israel for eighteen years. Jephthah was raised up as a judge and led war against them, defeating them with a great blow.

keyEvents.title: Saul Delivers Jabesh-Gilead from the Ammonites
keyEvents.description: Nahash, king of the Ammonites, besieged Jabesh-Gilead and demanded humiliating terms. Saul gathered Israel and defeated the Ammonites in a decisive battle that solidified his kingdom.

keyEvents.title: David's Conflict with the Ammonites
keyEvents.description: David sent messengers to Hanun, the new king of the Ammonites, to show goodwill after his father's death, but the messengers were humiliated. This triggered a major war in which David eventually captured the Ammonite capital, Rabbah.

keyEvents.title: Prophecies Against Ammon
keyEvents.description: Several prophets pronounced judgments against the Ammonites because of their hostility toward Israel, their pride, and their oppression. Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Amos proclaimed God's judgment upon them.

versions.summary: Ben-Ammi was the son of Lot and his youngest daughter, born after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. He became the ancestor of the Ammonites, a people who lived east of the Jordan and throughout Israel's history were neighbors, enemies, and rivals. The land of the Ammonites (often called 'Ammon') played a significant role in biblical accounts of Israel's conflicts and relationships with surrounding nations.

versions.summary: Ben-Ammi was the son of Lot and his youngest daughter, conceived after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:38). The name means 'my kinsman's son' in Hebrew and points to his origin. He is regarded as the ancestor of the Ammonites – a people who settled east of the Jordan with Rabbah (modern-day Amman) as their capital. The account of his birth serves an etiological function: it explains the origin of a neighboring people related to Israel through Lot, yet often in tense relations with the covenant people. Despite this kinship, God forbade the Israelites from attacking the Ammonite territory during the wilderness journey (Deut 2:19), testifying to a theological recognition of their right to the land. Throughout the period of the judges, the monarchy, and the prophetic literature, the Ammonites appear as a consistent actor – sometimes as oppressors, other times as targets of prophetic judgments. Ben-Ammi's figure thus connects the patriarchal era with the broader history of Israel and its neighboring peoples.

footnotes.text: The Ammonite god Milcom is mentioned in the Hebrew text as מַלְכָּם (Malkam), which can also be read as 'their king.' This ambiguity has led to debate among scholars about whether certain texts refer to a deity or a political ruler. The Septuagint consistently translates it as Melchom, confirming the interpretation of a divine name.

Excavations at Tell el-Umeiri southeast of Amman have uncovered a large fortification wall and seals bearing Ammonite personal names from the Iron Age, shedding light on Ammonite state organization and confirming the biblical portrayal of the Ammonites as an organized kingdom.

In historical geopolitics, Ammonite territory served as a buffer zone between the western Israelite tribes and the eastern desert nomads. Control over trade routes—especially the King's Highway (Deut 2:37; Num 21:22)—was a central cause of repeated conflicts between Israel and Ammon.
